owner_rulings.item_4: have a herdr worktree agent take care of that and fix it, i'm not going to be entering probas, i trust your panel of bjj experts and black belts to convene and figure the right probas and structure of nodes.

meta.panel: An LLM persona panel, NOT real coaches and NOT expert data. Ten voting personas, each an LLM (claude-opus-5-5) prompted with one unnamed coaching ARCHETYPE (systems, pragmatist, leg-skeptic, academic, gi-fundamentalist, guard-back, gi-guard-modern, unorthodox, gi-to-nogi, fhl-scrambler) and never with a person. Every persona cast an independent ballot on every request, blind to the others (40 agent runs: 10 archetypes x 4 batches of 28 requests).
meta.requests: 112 outcome tables: 5 new canonical tables for the moves the phase-1 panel re-homed (with a keep/remove ruling on the old-origin listing), and 107 per-listing tables for the away listings the phase-1 panel said deserve their own (own_table_at, weighted majority). The 8 deal_here listings need no new number: they deal the authored share with the authored table, and their verdicts are phase 1's judge ballots.
meta.aggregation: scripts/apply_listing_tables.py: Q3's expert_weight (specialty bonus x ruleset affinity, occurrence_moe.CONFIG, family = the Q3 family of the position-role the table is for). Success rate: weighted mean of non-null votes, rounded, 1..99, per frame; null only when more than half the weight votes null. Rows: within-branch shares, weighted mean per frame, pooled over the rated frames into ONE table for both rulesets (the corpus convention: outcome cells are equal across frames and the frame difference lives in the success rate); kept at >= 15% of a branch, 1-3 per branch, 3-5 in all; rescaled to the branch mass at the headline (no-gi) rate; occurrence_moe.floor_preserving_round to exactly 100. A kept destination the no-gi graph excludes is recorded per table. Verdicts: weighted plurality.
meta.rounds: ONE round. No deliberation and no adversarial verify pass ran (the phase-1 attempt at a deliberation round was refused and then stopped; see calibration/origin_coherence.json meta). Deterministic checks replace the verify pass: every request answered, 3-5 rows, sums, legal role-node destinations, a success and a miss row, no-gi exclusions honoured, and the content gates.

systems.old_origin_reason: The sweep needs both feet loaded on the hips; from closed guard you must first open into feet-on-hips, which is a separate transition, not this move.
systems.reason: This is the balloon sweep's true home, so it stays near canonical; it is lower in no-gi because wrist ties replace the sleeve and collar pull that drives them overhead.

pragmatist.old_origin_reason: From closed guard you must open the legs and set both feet on the hips first, which is this position; it is not a closed-guard attempt.
pragmatist.reason: Feet on hips is the balloon sweep's true launch point; collar and sleeve grips make it better in gi than with wrist ties in no-gi.

leg-skeptic.old_origin_reason: Nobody launches a balloon with their ankles crossed: you open and put feet on hips first, which is this position, not closed guard.
leg-skeptic.reason: Both feet in the hips with a pull is where the balloon actually lives; sleeve or collar grips make it better in the gi, and in no-gi you get stacked more.

academic.old_origin_reason: From closed guard you must first open into feet on hips, which is its own state, so listing it there skips a step.
academic.reason: Feet on hips is where the launch actually happens; gi collar and sleeve grips make the pull-over more reliable than no-gi wrist ties.

gi-fundamentalist.old_origin_reason: From closed guard you must first open and put both feet on the hips; the balloon itself is a feet-on-hips attack, not a closed-guard one.
gi-fundamentalist.reason: Both feet already on the hips is the balloon's real home; collar and sleeve grips make the overhead launch much more reliable in the gi than wrist control in no-gi.

guard-back.old_origin_reason: From closed guard you open, place both feet on the hips and launch as they posture forward; it is a real if rare attempt from there.
guard-back.reason: Feet on hips is the balloon sweep's true launch; sleeve and collar grips make it much easier in gi, while no-gi wrist control lets more opponents land on their feet or pass.

gi-guard-modern.old_origin_reason: Opening closed guard to feet-on-hips and launching when the opponent postures is still a taught balloon-sweep entry.
gi-guard-modern.reason: Feet on hips is the native balloon-sweep frame; gi sleeve/collar grips keep the connection through the launch, no-gi wrist ties slip far more.

unorthodox.old_origin_reason: From closed guard you must first open into feet-on-hips, which the graph models as its own transition; listing it there is a teleport.
unorthodox.reason: Both feet on the hips is the balloon sweep's real launch position, so it keeps canonical-level odds in the gi, where sleeve and collar grips steer the throw; no-gi wrist control is slipperier.

gi-to-nogi.old_origin_reason: Still drilled from closed guard as the guard opens when the opponent stands and both feet go straight to the hips.
gi-to-nogi.reason: Feet on hips is the true launch pad; collar and sleeve grips make the overhead lift reliable, no-gi wrist grips lose a lot.

fhl-scrambler.old_origin_reason: From closed guard you must first open and get both feet on the hips, which is the feet-on-hips state; listing it at closed guard skips that step.
fhl-scrambler.reason: Both feet on the hips is the sweep's real launch pad; sleeve and collar grips make the pull more reliable in the gi than wrist grips in no-gi.

systems.old_origin_reason: The buggy-choke defender is the man physically on top of side control; shrimping to guard is not a real attempt from that seat.
systems.reason: Side control bottom is the home of the elbow-knee escape; most wins are half guard first, no-gi slightly easier without lapel crossface pins.

pragmatist.old_origin_reason: The buggy-choke seat is not a place anyone shrimps to guard from; that exchange is about the choke, and listing a guard-recovery escape there is a mistake.
pragmatist.reason: The bread-and-butter side control escape: frame, shrimp, knee in; most recoveries are half guard, a stalled one leaves you pinned, a lazy shrimp gets mounted. No-gi top lacks the collar crossface, so a touch easier.

leg-skeptic.old_origin_reason: Nobody elbow-escapes out of their own buggy choke; when it stalls you unlock and you are just side-control bottom, which is where this move actually lives.
leg-skeptic.reason: Shrimp-and-knee-in is the bread-and-butter side control escape; gi crossface and belt grips make the pin stickier, so a touch under the buggy-choke anchor.

academic.old_origin_reason: In this graph buggy-choke/bottom is the player being choked, who is physically on top of side control; there is no guard to recover from there, so the listing is a role error.
academic.reason: Side control bottom is the textbook home of the shrimp-and-knee-in guard recovery; often ends in half guard rather than full guard, and a mistimed turn concedes mount. Slightly better in no-gi with no collar crossface.

gi-fundamentalist.old_origin_reason: Buggy-choke/bottom is the man being choked from on top of side control; shrimping to guard is not an escape from there, the defence is to posture or step over.
gi-fundamentalist.reason: The shrimp-and-knee-in is THE fundamental side control escape; gi crossface and lapel grips keep it a bit harder than at buggy choke; most recoveries are half guard, a miss stays pinned, a sloppy shrimp gives up mount.

guard-back.old_origin_reason: The buggy-choke defender is the side-control top player; they have no guard to recover, so an elbow escape to guard is not a real option there.
guard-back.reason: The textbook shrimp/knee-in re-guard from side control; gi collar/belt grips make the pin a bit stickier, and the top player stepping to mount is the classic punish.

gi-guard-modern.old_origin_reason: The buggy choke is a bottom-side-control attack, so its bottom seat is the choked player who is physically on top; there is no guard to recover from there.
gi-guard-modern.reason: Classic shrimp-and-knee-in guard recovery under side control; gi crossface and collar grips pin harder, no-gi is slipperier to escape.

unorthodox.old_origin_reason: buggy-choke/bottom is the man on top being choked; he has no guard to recover, so the listing is a role error.
unorthodox.reason: The elbow-knee shrimp is THE side control re-guard; slightly below the anchor vs a set crossface, a bit easier in no-gi with sweat and no lapel pin; the knee-cut to mount is the usual punish.

gi-to-nogi.old_origin_reason: The buggy-choke defender is physically the side-control top player; shrimping to recover guard is not a real answer there, so the listing is a mistake.
gi-to-nogi.reason: The textbook frame-and-shrimp guard recovery; gi collar and belt grips pin a little harder than no-gi, where sweat helps the hip escape.

fhl-scrambler.old_origin_reason: The bottom player in a stalled buggy choke is already turned in and routinely abandons it to frame and shrimp back to guard; that is a real chain.
fhl-scrambler.reason: The textbook frame-and-shrimp re-guard from side control; slightly easier in no-gi with no collar or belt grips pinning you, and the top player steps to mount as you turn.

systems.old_origin_reason: The lumberjack is the sit-up double-heel chop against a standing opponent; the half-guard underhook version described there is a different sweep, so listing it at half guard is a mislabel.
systems.reason: From seated guard against a standing passer, grabbing both heels and driving the shoulder through the knees is the actual lumberjack; a sprawl puts you in a front headlock.

pragmatist.old_origin_reason: There is no half-guard lumberjack; the half-guard version described is an underhook sweep under the wrong name.
pragmatist.reason: The lumberjack is a sit-up-guard double-heel sweep against a standing opponent; pant grips help in the gi, and diving for ankles in no-gi gets sprawled into front headlocks.

leg-skeptic.old_origin_reason: The lumberjack is a double-ankle chop against a standing passer; the half-guard underhook sweep listed there is a different move filed under the wrong name.
leg-skeptic.reason: Sit up, grab both heels and drive the shoulder through; pant cuffs help in gi. Putting your head low invites the sprawl to front headlock, more so in no-gi.

academic.old_origin_reason: The lumberjack means grabbing both heels of a standing opponent and chopping them down, which you can't do from half guard bottom; the half-guard underhook sweep is a different move.
academic.reason: Seated against a standing passer, you cup both heels and drive forward, they sit down and you come up on top; your head is exposed while you reach, so a snap-down to front headlock is the counter, more so in no-gi.

gi-fundamentalist.old_origin_reason: The lumberjack is a two-heel chop against a standing opponent; from half guard the underhook sweeps are other moves (old school, plan B), so listing it there is a mistake.
gi-fundamentalist.reason: This is the real lumberjack: catch both heels of a standing opponent, drive the hips and come up on top; driving your head in invites the sprawl and front headlock, more so in no-gi.

guard-back.old_origin_reason: The lumberjack is the two-heel sweep against a standing opponent; the half-guard underhook sweep listed there is the old school/dogfight family, not this move.
guard-back.reason: From seated guard against a standing passer you grab both heels and drive, so it is above the half-guard rate; driving head-first exposes the guillotine, and a freed leg steps into HQ. Pant grips help in gi.

gi-guard-modern.old_origin_reason: The lumberjack is a both-heels grab and drive against a standing passer; from half guard bottom the passer's leg is trapped and nobody is standing, so that listing misnames an underhook sweep.
gi-guard-modern.reason: Sit up, grab both heels (pant cuffs in gi), drive the shoulder into the hips and chop them down; the sprawl to a front headlock is the standard counter.

unorthodox.old_origin_reason: The lumberjack needs both heels of a standing opponent; from bottom half guard against a kneeling passer it cannot be done, and the half-guard version is really the old-school sweep.
unorthodox.reason: Sitting up to cup both heels and chop a standing opponent down is the true lumberjack, so slightly above the misfiled half-guard odds; heel cups work in both rulesets.

gi-to-nogi.old_origin_reason: Against a kneeling half-guard passer there are no standing heels to chop; the underhook sweep from half guard is the old-school or dogfight sweep, a different move.
gi-to-nogi.reason: The lumberjack is the seated-guard double-heel grab against a standing opponent: block the knees, push forward, fell them and come up on top. Pant-cuff grips make it a little easier in the gi.

fhl-scrambler.old_origin_reason: The heel-grab lumberjack needs a standing opponent and seated hips; the half-guard underhook sweep described there is really the old school/dogfight, so listing it there is a mistake.
fhl-scrambler.reason: Grab both heels from seated, drive forward and they fall back, which leaves you passing; shooting your head in hands a front headlock to anyone who sprawls, more so in no-gi.

systems.old_origin_reason: A butterfly waiter (under-knee lift with a hook) is a real, minor attempt; its small share and current table there are fine.
systems.reason: The waiter is the signature deep-half sweep: lift the leg like a tray and come up on top, usually into half guard or a scramble to side control; the punish is getting flattened and passed.

pragmatist.old_origin_reason: The waiter is a deep-half leg-scoop sweep; the butterfly listing is just a butterfly hook sweep under the wrong name.
pragmatist.reason: Deep half is where the waiter sweep actually lives; it is a staple and beats the canonical butterfly odds, slightly better in the gi where opponents scramble less.

leg-skeptic.old_origin_reason: The waiter is the under-the-hips tray lift of the leg from deep half; the butterfly version described is just a hook sweep with a different name, and nobody attempts a waiter from butterfly.
leg-skeptic.reason: Deep half is the waiter's home, and it converts better there than the butterfly calibration suggests. You usually come up still caught in their half guard.

academic.old_origin_reason: A minor butterfly-guard version exists, scooping the posted leg while elevating with the hooks, and the current butterfly table describes it correctly.
academic.reason: Deep half is the waiter's true home: lifting the far leg like a tray and rolling them usually brings you up in half guard or side control, with a backstep pass as the main counter.

gi-fundamentalist.old_origin_reason: Butterfly players do dive under the far leg into the waiter grip; it is a rare but genuine attempt there, and its butterfly table still fits.
gi-fundamentalist.reason: The waiter is deep half's signature sweep: lift the far ankle and come up in his legs or to side control; friction keeps you under the hips in the gi, and a sit-through or flattening is the punish.

guard-back.old_origin_reason: Diving under the leg from butterfly or shin-to-shin into the waiter is a real low-share entry in no-gi, so its butterfly table can stay.
guard-back.reason: Deep half is the waiter's home (hand under the near leg like a tray), so success is above the butterfly calibration; you usually come up into their half guard; backstep passes are the punish.

gi-guard-modern.old_origin_reason: Rare but real: from butterfly you can dive a waiter grip under a posted leg and lift, so the small butterfly listing and its table stay valid.
gi-guard-modern.reason: Deep half is the waiter's true home: lift the far leg and tip them, usually coming up in their half guard; gi pant and belt grips hold the lift better than a sweaty no-gi leg.

unorthodox.old_origin_reason: A waiter grip needs you under their hips; from butterfly you must first dive to deep half or SLX, so the butterfly listing is a naming error.
unorthodox.reason: Deep-half waiter is the sweep's real home and one of the highest-percentage sweeps in the game; a pant grip helps slightly in gi.

gi-to-nogi.old_origin_reason: From butterfly guard the underhook-and-hook lift is just the butterfly sweep; a waiter sweep there means first dropping into deep half, which is a separate transition.
gi-to-nogi.reason: The waiter is a deep-half sweep at heart, scooping the far leg like a tray, and it is clearly stronger here than from butterfly. Most sweeps come up in their half guard; in no-gi the back-step escape is more common.

fhl-scrambler.old_origin_reason: Dropping under from butterfly and scooping the far leg is a real, if rare, waiter entry; 2% fits.
fhl-scrambler.reason: Deep half is the waiter's real home: tray hand on the far leg, tip them and come up, often still caught in half guard. Pants grips help the lift in gi.

systems.old_origin_reason: The X pass is a standing step-across vs an open/seated guard; with a leg trapped in half guard the X step cannot happen, so that listing is really a knee-cut/crossface pass.
systems.reason: Its true home: grip knees/pants, step out and drive across; slightly lower in no-gi where knee/ankle grips slip and leg entries punish the step.

pragmatist.old_origin_reason: With a leg trapped in half guard you cannot make the X-pass step; that half-guard 'X pass' is a hip-switch/knee-cut under another name.
pragmatist.reason: The X pass is a standing open-guard speed pass; pant grips help a little in gi.

leg-skeptic.old_origin_reason: The X pass is a standing open-guard pass; a crossface pass from top half guard is a knee cut wearing the wrong name, and nobody X-passes from there.
leg-skeptic.reason: This is the X pass's real home; pant/knee grips help in gi, and in no-gi stepping around the legs hands a leg locker an outside ashi.

academic.old_origin_reason: The crossface diagonal-angle version from top half guard is a real, if minor, variant, and its existing table is coherent there.
academic.reason: This is the classic standing X pass against an open guard: knee control, a diagonal step back and around, landing side or knee-on-belly. Odds sit near canonical in both rulesets.

gi-fundamentalist.old_origin_reason: In half guard your leg is trapped, so there is no knee to push down and no angle to step around; the half-guard crossface-and-cut is the knee slice, which is already listed there.
gi-fundamentalist.reason: The X pass is a standing angle pass against an open guard; from here it runs at the canonical rate, a little lower in no-gi where the knee push slips.

guard-back.old_origin_reason: The X-pass steps across two free legs; with one leg trapped in half guard the motion is a knee slice or crossface pass, not an X-pass.
guard-back.reason: Open guard is the X-pass's real home: post on the knee and step across in an X, landing in side control or knee-on-belly; a miss resets, they catch half guard, or the passer gets swept in the scramble.

gi-guard-modern.old_origin_reason: The X pass is a standing cross-step pass against an open guard; the half-guard crossface drive is a knee-cut or pressure pass, so listing it there is a mistake.
gi-guard-modern.reason: Its true home: the passer grips the knee or pants and cross-steps past the legs; gi sleeve grips let the guard player stall a little more.

unorthodox.old_origin_reason: The X Pass is a standing step-across pass against an open seated or butterfly guard. When half guard has trapped your leg there is no X step, so the half guard listing is a misfile.
unorthodox.reason: X Pass belongs to open guard, where it is a standing speed pass. Gi grips slow it slightly, and a re-guard or a caught half guard are the usual misses.

gi-to-nogi.old_origin_reason: The X-pass is a standing speed pass against an open guard; the crossface-diagonal motion from top half guard is a knee-slice or smash pass, not an X-pass.
gi-to-nogi.reason: Its true home: step across the legs in an X while controlling a knee or pant; sleeve and collar grips slow it more in gi.

fhl-scrambler.old_origin_reason: The crossface/angle half-guard variant in the overview is a rare but real attempt from top half guard; its 1% share is right.
fhl-scrambler.reason: The X pass is a standing open-guard speed pass: cross-step past the legs to side control or knee on belly; misses reset to open guard.

systems.reason: The leg is already entangled, so switching to 50-50 when they step or rotate is easier than entering from inverted guard; no-gi defenders fight it harder.

pragmatist.reason: Switching from ashi to 50-50 when they step or turn is a staple and easier than from inverted guard since you already own the leg; in no-gi they clear the knee line more often.

leg-skeptic.reason: Switching an existing ashi to 50-50 is a short hop compared with inverting into it; most no-gi ashi players go saddle instead, but the switch itself works.

academic.reason: Switching from ashi to 50-50 when the knee line comes inside is a core leg-lock transition and easier than inverting into it. No-gi defenders extract early because of heel hook danger, matching the canonical gap.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: The leg is already entangled, so swinging into 50-50 beats the canonical inverted-guard entry; gi friction makes the triangle of legs stickier; a freed leg can be passed.

guard-back.reason: The leg is already entangled, so switching to 50-50 when they turn or step is short and beats the inverted entry; gi pant grips hold it better than sweaty no-gi legs.

gi-guard-modern.reason: You already control the leg, so swinging the outside leg across to 50-50 is a short step; pants grips make it stickier in the gi, and in no-gi the leg slips and the inside position gets contested.

unorthodox.reason: Already entangled, swinging the outside leg over to 50-50 is easy, so above the inverted anchor; no-gi players prefer the saddle and backstep out more.

gi-to-nogi.reason: With the leg already entangled, switching to 50-50 as they try to free it is a small step, well above the inverted-guard origin. Pants grips make it stickier in the gi.

fhl-scrambler.reason: You are already entangled, so switching to 50-50 when they rotate or step is far easier than from inverted guard; the counters are a leg reversal or a pass as the legs come apart.

systems.reason: K-guard is a designed 50-50 entry with the inside leg already threaded; the pass during the inversion is the main counter.

pragmatist.reason: K-guard is built as a leg-entanglement entry and 50-50 is one of its main exits, better in no-gi where they cannot pant-grip to block the invert; a slow invert gets passed.

leg-skeptic.reason: K-guard exists to feed 50-50 and the backside; a modern no-gi staple, a bit above the inverted-guard anchor.

academic.reason: K-guard is designed as a 50-50 entry (inside hook plus a hip angle under the leg), so it is above the inverted-guard rate; a passer who stays heavy and steps around beats it.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: K-guard is built to feed the 50-50 entry, so it beats the canonical rate; a stalled entry stays in K-guard or opens up; a top player who steps out can pass.

guard-back.reason: K-guard is built to enter 50-50 by inverting under the near leg, so it beats the canonical rate; a pressure pass while you are inverted is the counter.

gi-guard-modern.reason: K-guard is built for this kind of leg entry, so odds sit above the inverted-guard canonical; a backstep or pass is the counter.

unorthodox.reason: K-guard is a dedicated 50-50 and sankaku entry, well above the anchor in no-gi where it was built; gi pant grips let the passer pin the hips and pass more.

gi-to-nogi.reason: K-guard is built to feed leg entanglements, and 50-50 is one of its main exits. Mistiming the invert lets them backstep or pass.

fhl-scrambler.reason: K-guard is built to spin under into the legs, so 50-50 is a standard entry here and sharper in the no-gi leg-lock game; inverting under a heavy passer gets you passed.

systems.reason: Dead orchard is already an arm-in anaconda-family grip, so locking the anaconda is a short step; keeps the canonical gi-over-no-gi edge.

pragmatist.reason: The anaconda grip is already locked in this position, so finishing the roll into anaconda control is the expected completion and above the front-headlock baseline.

leg-skeptic.reason: Dead orchard already is an anaconda-family grip, so locking the anaconda from it beats the front-headlock anchor.

academic.reason: The arm-in grip is already locked, so this is above the front-headlock rate; a failed gator roll leaves you under in half guard.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: The arm-in grip is already locked, so getting to anaconda control is well above canonical; a lost grip falls back to front headlock, a failed roll puts you under.

guard-back.reason: Dead orchard is already the anaconda grip with positional control, so locking the anaconda is easier than from front headlock; a roll-through is the counter.

gi-guard-modern.reason: You already hold the anaconda-family arm-in grip, so the switch is a grip refinement above the canonical; gi friction keeps the lock from slipping.

unorthodox.reason: Dead orchard already has the arm-in grip, so settling it into the anaconda finish is well above the anchor; the sit-through counter is a little more common in no-gi.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Dead orchard is already an arm-in anaconda-family control, so locking the anaconda finish grip is above the front-headlock rate. Gi friction keeps the arm in.

fhl-scrambler.reason: The anaconda grip is already locked here, so finishing it beats the front-headlock rate; the gi-over-no-gi gap from the canonical holds, and a sloppy roll lets them come up on top.

systems.reason: From the whizzer you must first snap the head down and thread under the near arm; workable but less set up than a front headlock.

pragmatist.reason: The whizzer is over the arm, but the anaconda needs to thread under it from the front, so you have to convert to a headlock first; a real but secondary option.

leg-skeptic.reason: The whizzer arm is on the arm, not the head; you only get the anaconda when they drop their head to come up, so well under the anchor.

academic.reason: From the whizzer you must first switch to the head and thread under the arm, so this is well below the canonical rate; the defender's single-leg pressure continues while you transition.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: From a whizzer you still have to snap the head and thread the arm, so it is well below canonical; gi friction keeps the head-and-arm a little better; failed rolls land you underneath.

guard-back.reason: From the whizzer you first have to snap the head down and thread under the arm, one step short of front headlock; that costs a lot, and a re-shot counter puts you on bottom.

gi-guard-modern.reason: An overhook is the wrong arm configuration, so you must snap the head down and re-thread under the arm first, which keeps odds low; a missed lock usually resets the whizzer.

unorthodox.reason: From the whizzer you must first snap the head down to get arm-in, so below the anchor; diving with their underhook free gives them the come-up or your back.

gi-to-nogi.reason: The whizzer-to-anaconda against a player coming up on the underhook is real, but you must switch off the overhook first. Letting go of the whizzer can give up the sweep or the back.

fhl-scrambler.reason: You have to move from the whizzer to a front headlock and thread the arm before you can choke, so it lands far less often; a failed anaconda roll leaves you on your back with them in your guard.

systems.reason: You must sit up from the feet-on-hips distance to drag, so it lands far less than from closed guard; no-gi wrists are easier to drag.

pragmatist.reason: From feet on hips you must sit up to drag, so it is a back take or wrestle-up rather than a closed-guard sweep; lower than canonical, and more common in no-gi.

leg-skeptic.reason: You have to sit up and close distance before you can drag, so well under the closed-guard anchor; no-gi seated arm drags to the back are common.

academic.reason: You must sit up off the hips to drag, which gives the passer a window, so this is well below the closed-guard rate. Arm drags carry over well to no-gi, where there are no sleeve grips to strip.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: With feet on hips you are farther from the arm than in closed guard, and gi grips on the pants make the drag harder; well below canonical; sitting up to drag can open the pass.

guard-back.reason: Seated open-guard arm drags work when they reach, but without closed guard's posture break it is below the canonical rate; it is more common and more effective in no-gi, where there are no lapel grips to stall it.

gi-guard-modern.reason: From open guard you must sit up before you can drag, so odds are well below closed guard; the arm drag is a no-gi staple, and gi collar grips blunt the sit-up.

unorthodox.reason: You must sit up off the hips before you can drag, so well below the closed-guard anchor; the arm drag is a no-gi wrestling weapon, and sitting up early lets them pass.

gi-to-nogi.reason: From distance you have to sit up into the drag, so it is well below the closed-guard origin. No-gi arm drags flow better; in the gi, sleeves and collar grips anchor the top player.

fhl-scrambler.reason: At feet-on-hips distance you must drop a foot and sit up to drag, so it lands well below the closed-guard rate; the no-gi 2-on-1 drag to the back is a staple, and dropping your feet lets a ready passer through.

systems.reason: Pulling the arm out of a locked gable kills the arm-in choke but usually leaves you in front headlock or turtle; the top player spins behind on a slow extraction; sweat helps a little in no-gi.

pragmatist.reason: Pulling the trapped arm out of a locked anaconda is a low-odds survival move; success only gets you to a head-only front headlock or turtle, and a late pull feeds the back or a darce switch.

leg-skeptic.reason: Pulling the arm out of an arm-in choke is harder than clearing a side-control underhook; a half-win often leaves you in front headlock, and turning wrong gives the back. Sweat helps a little in no-gi.

academic.reason: Pulling the arm out of a locked gable is harder than clearing a side-control underhook; a freed arm usually leaves you headlocked or turtled, and the common punish is a switch to the darce side.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Pulling the trapped arm out of a locked anaconda is hard; a freed arm leaves turtle or a bare front headlock, and the top man spins to the back or rewraps a guillotine; sweat helps slightly in no-gi.

leg-skeptic.reason: Switching between anaconda and darce with head and arm already controlled is a staple 10th Planet chain, so it beats a cold darce from turtle.

academic.reason: With head and arm already controlled, switching to the darce side beats a cold entry from turtle; the lapels get in the way of the thread in gi, and a defender who rolls through comes up on top in your half guard.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Switching from the anaconda-family grip to the darce is a standard chain with the head and arm already caught; lapels and friction make threading harder in the gi.

guard-back.reason: Head and arm are already trapped, so the anaconda-to-darce switch when they move the arm beats a cold darce from turtle; a botched switch lets them roll through on top.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Already arm-in on the head, switching the thread to a darce is a short front-headlock switch; collar friction and own-collar defences slow it a little in gi.

unorthodox.reason: Switching from the anaconda-family dead orchard to the darce is a natural arm-in switch with the head already controlled; it is a no-gi staple and threads more slowly through gi friction.

gi-to-nogi.reason: From dead orchard you already control the head and arm, so re-threading to the darce side is a quick switch within the anaconda family; the lapel gets in the way of the gi darce.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Head and arm are already in place, so threading to the darce is a short switch within the arm-in family and above canonical; gi lapels and friction slow the thread.

systems.reason: Dropping to both legs from behind is a high-percentage rear double, but you land behind them (turtle or back) more than in front; switches and hand-fighting stop some.

pragmatist.reason: From behind this is a rear double: high percentage, lands them face-down; sweat lets more slip in no-gi.

leg-skeptic.reason: From behind this is a rear double or mat return, not a front double; the drop works well, but you land behind them on turtle or the back, not in side control.

academic.reason: A rear double from behind cannot be sprawled, but the opponent lands facing away, so it finishes in turtle or the back more often than side control; somewhat below the canonical finish.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: From behind, this is a rear double: drop, collect both legs and drive them forward, which usually lands them in turtle or gives the back rather than side control; it runs below the finish rate because the penetration step is not done yet.

guard-back.reason: Dropping to both legs from behind and driving forward is a strong rear takedown, but it lands them turtled or flat, not in side control, and gives them time to turn in; a slipperier rear lock costs a little in no-gi.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Lifting and dropping an opponent from behind is a high-percentage finish, if below the canonical penetrated double; gi belt grips steady the lift.

unorthodox.reason: A rear double from behind lands most opponents face-down on turtle or flat for the back. It is a little below a front double's finish because they can turn in or post.

gi-to-nogi.reason: From behind it is a rear double: they fall forward to turtle or give up the back, not side control, and it stays high-percentage.

fhl-scrambler.reason: From behind, the leg drive lands them turtled or flat with you on the back rather than in front side control; slightly below the in-front finish rate.

systems.reason: The posted leg leaves a knee lane, but the framing arm feeds the 3-4 mount's triangle when the escape stalls.

pragmatist.reason: Elbow-knee into the side the top already opened; usually lands half guard. Turning too far hands the back, otherwise they settle full mount.

leg-skeptic.reason: Posted leg leaves a real knee-elbow lane, about as good as a low mount escape; a sloppy turn lets them square up to full mount.

academic.reason: Top is already half off the mount, so the elbow-knee escape finds a leg to trap; half guard is the usual landing, a re-squared full mount the usual counter.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: The raised leg of a 3/4 mount leaves room for the elbow-knee; usually recovers half guard; a stuffed attempt re-seals mount, over-turning gives the back.

guard-back.reason: The open side of 3/4 mount gives the elbow-knee escape a real gap; mostly ends in half guard, and turning too far hands them technical mount.

gi-guard-modern.reason: The posted foot leaves the knee-elbow lane open, so the escape lands mostly half guard first; a miss lets them settle into full mount.

unorthodox.reason: The loose leg side of 3/4 mount is the easiest knee to recover, so roughly at the anchor; mostly half guard first, and they re-square to full mount when it fails badly.

gi-to-nogi.reason: The posted leg leaves a knee-elbow lane, usually to half guard first. The top player re-centres to full mount or follows the turn to technical mount.

fhl-scrambler.reason: The posted leg leaves a gap for the elbow-knee escape, so this is easier than from full mount, and it mostly ends in half guard; the counter is the top player settling back to full mount.

systems.reason: One leg is already trapped so reframing to knee shield or full guard is realistic; the shrimp also frees the leg for the passer.

pragmatist.reason: Already holding a leg, so getting the elbow back and shrimping to knee shield or full guard is realistic; shrimping off a free leg lets them pass to side control.

leg-skeptic.reason: Leg already trapped so re-framing to knee shield or half is realistic, but flattened under a crossface the shrimp often just gets you passed.

academic.reason: Re-framing and shrimping off a crossface rebuilds the knee shield more often than full guard; the shrimp frees the trapped leg for the pass when it fails.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Already holding a leg, so the elbow-knee frame mostly rebuilds the knee shield or half guard; gi crossface pressure keeps more attempts flattened; shrimping out invites the pass.

guard-back.reason: A leg is already trapped, so shrimping to get the elbow and knee back inside rebuilds half guard or a knee shield; freeing the leg while shrimping gets you passed.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Re-framing from flat half guard rebuilds knee shield or full guard; the crossface (stronger with a gi collar grip) keeps many attempts pinned, and moving opens the pass.

unorthodox.reason: A leg is already trapped, so getting the elbow back in mostly rebuilds a knee shield; when the shrimp opens the hip they slide the leg free and pass.

gi-to-nogi.reason: A leg is already trapped, so getting back to your side with a knee shield is close. The cost is that shrimping can free the leg and hand the top player the pass.

fhl-scrambler.reason: One leg is already trapped, so re-framing gets back to a working half guard or knee shield; if the shrimp is late, the top player frees the knee and passes to side control.

systems.reason: Knees in the armpits leave almost no elbow-knee space; turning to shrimp hands top the S-mount.

pragmatist.reason: Elbows are pinned above your head, so a direct guard recovery is rare; the common good outcome is just getting back to low mount, and turning into it feeds S-mount.

leg-skeptic.reason: Knees in the armpits leave no elbow-knee connection; you mostly just push them back to low mount, and turning feeds the S-mount armbar.

academic.reason: Knees under the armpits remove the elbow-knee channel; most attempts only knock top back to low mount, and turning exposes the arm to S-mount.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Knees at the armpits leave no room for the elbow to reach the knee; low odds, the best miss is dropping them back to low mount, and turning exposes the arm to S-mount.

guard-back.reason: With knees in your armpits there is no elbow-to-knee connection; the best usual result is pushing them back to low mount, and extended arms feed S-mount.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Knees in the armpits leave almost no elbow-to-knee space, so odds sit well below the canonical; partial progress only drops them back to low mount, and turning feeds S-mount.

unorthodox.reason: With knees at the armpits the elbows cannot reach the knees; most attempts only drag them back to low mount, and pushing on the high leg feeds S-mount.

gi-to-nogi.reason: With the knees in your armpits there is no elbow-to-knee frame, so it rarely works. Turning to your side feeds the S-mount and the armbar.

fhl-scrambler.reason: With the knees in your armpits the elbows cannot get inside, so it often only pushes them back to low mount; pushing on the knees exposes an arm to S-mount.

systems.reason: Freeing the trapped elbow and shrimping away is a legit kesa escape but the head-and-arm clamp holds most attempts; top steps to mount as hips move.

pragmatist.reason: Frame on the hip, shrimp away and stuff a knee in; works but kesa is heavy, especially with gi collar and sleeve grips, and a scramble often lets them step to mount.

leg-skeptic.reason: Hip frame and shrimp to re-guard works on scarf hold but head-and-arm control kills a lot of attempts, worse in the gi; turning in invites the step to mount.

academic.reason: Frame on the hip and shrimp to insert a knee is the standard scarf-hold escape, but the head-and-arm pin is heavy; the sleeve and belt grips hold it better in gi, and top switches to mount as you turn in.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Scarf hold traps the head and near arm, so the frame-and-shrimp gains less than vs side control; when it works it is usually half guard; space you make can be used to step to mount.

guard-back.reason: Freeing the near elbow and shrimping to put a knee in is the standard scarf-hold re-guard; gi arm and collar control make it harder, and a follow to side control or mount is the punish.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Framing on the hip and shrimping to get a knee in usually recovers half guard; scarf-hold pressure with gi sleeve and collar control stops many attempts, and they switch to mount when you turn in.

unorthodox.reason: Kesa's head-and-arm hug blunts the frame, so below the anchor; turning in to get a knee back works more in no-gi, and the classic punish is the switch to mount.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Frame on the hip, shrimp and insert the knee. A gi sleeve-and-collar scarf hold is much stickier than a no-gi one, where the trapped arm slips free.

fhl-scrambler.reason: A hip escape to get the knee in mostly recovers half guard; scarf hold is much leakier without the collar and sleeve grips in no-gi; the top player switches to side control or steps to mount.

systems.reason: Knee on belly is the least stable pin; push the knee and shrimp recovers open guard often, but top slides to mount off the push.

pragmatist.reason: Knee on belly is a high, loose pin, so push the knee and shrimp to open guard is a real escape; the miss is they drop back to side control or slide to mount. No collar grip in no-gi makes KOB harder to keep.

leg-skeptic.reason: Knee on belly is a high, unstable pin, so pushing the knee and shrimping is the standard escape and lands near the anchor; the counter is the slide to mount.

academic.reason: Pushing the knee off and shrimping recovers open guard fairly often because there is space under the knee; a slow shrimp lets top slide the knee across to mount. In no-gi there is no collar grip to keep the knee posted.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Knee on belly is less stable than side control, so pushing the knee and shrimping recovers guard fairly often; gi collar and pants grips hold it better than no-gi; the classic counter slides the knee to mount.

guard-back.reason: Knee on belly has a high base, so framing the shin and shrimping recovers guard about as often as at the canonical origin; sliding to mount is the punish.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Knee on belly is a high, unstable pin, so pushing the knee and shrimping recovers guard often; collar-and-belt grips steady it in the gi, and a pushed knee often slides to mount.

unorthodox.reason: Knee on belly is the least stable pin; push the knee and shrimp re-guards a bit above the anchor, more in no-gi without collar/pant grips; the punish is sliding the knee to mount.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Knee-on-belly is unstable, so pushing the knee and shrimping often recovers guard. The classic punish is the top player sliding to mount, and collar-and-belt grips hold it better in the gi.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Pushing the knee and shrimping away is the primary knee-on-belly escape and recovers open guard often; without the collar and belt grips, knee-on-belly is harder to ride in no-gi.

systems.reason: Low hips and the underarm base make the shrimp hard; moving the near elbow exposes the far arm or lets top step to mount.

pragmatist.reason: Same frame-and-shrimp as kesa, slightly harder because the arm under the far armpit kills the bridge; failure keeps you pinned, overcommitting gets you mounted.

leg-skeptic.reason: Trapped near arm means one frame, so it is well below the anchor; the isolated arm is what they punish when you turn.

academic.reason: The isolated far arm leaves only one frame, so the escape is worse than from kesa; turning into the top player feeds mount or the trapped arm.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: The trapped arm removes one frame, so the elbow escape is below its canonical rate; mostly ends in half guard; pulling the arm free carelessly gives mount or the straight armbar.

guard-back.reason: The trapped far arm leaves only one usable frame, so it is harder than plain kesa; working the escape exposes that arm to a lock or a step to mount.

gi-guard-modern.reason: With the near arm trapped, you have one frame fewer than in kesa, so odds are slightly lower; you still mostly recover half guard, or they step to mount.

unorthodox.reason: With the near arm trapped you have only one frame, so well below the anchor; turning away exposes the trapped arm to the armbar or the step to mount.

gi-to-nogi.reason: With the near arm trapped, one frame is gone and the escape is weaker than from side control. The isolated arm is the counter risk.

fhl-scrambler.reason: The trapped arm leaves only one frame, so it is harder than from kesa; shrimping with that arm isolated feeds the armbar or a step to mount.

systems.reason: Asymmetric base gives a lane under the posted leg like a standard mount escape; turning to the side invites technical mount.

pragmatist.reason: Standard elbow-knee toward the posted-leg side; close to the mount escape, mostly yielding half guard, with the usual mount re-settle or back exposure on a bad turn.

leg-skeptic.reason: Posted-leg side gives a genuine knee-elbow lane, roughly a standard mount escape rate.

academic.reason: The posted leg offers a directional elbow-knee path to half guard; when it is mistimed, top just squares back up to full mount.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Elbow-knee toward the knee-down side of the asymmetric mount is the textbook route; near canonical odds; a miss leaves the mount, turning too far gives the back.

guard-back.reason: Escaping toward the posted-leg side uses the uneven weight; usually it ends in half guard or lockdown, and they square back up to full mount if it is late.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Escaping toward the posted leg recovers half guard or lockdown like a 3/4-mount escape; a miss lets them square into full mount.

unorthodox.reason: The posted leg is a real escape lane, so near the anchor; in no-gi the knee you recover is often triple-locked into the lockdown straight away.

gi-to-nogi.reason: The knee-elbow works toward the posted-leg side, as from 3/4 mount. The top player re-mounts or follows you to technical mount.

fhl-scrambler.reason: With the weight uneven, the elbow-knee escape toward the knee-down side works about as well as from 3/4 mount, and it ends in half guard or lockdown; the top player squares back up to mount.

systems.reason: Already on your side with top one step from the back; wrong-way shrimps feed the back take or the near-arm armbar.

pragmatist.reason: You are on your side with a leg behind you, so elbow-knee to recover half guard is the right escape, but every bad turn feeds the back take or the armbar that technical mount exists for.

leg-skeptic.reason: You are already on your side with their leg by your head; re-guarding is possible but every miss leaks the back or the arm.

academic.reason: Technical mount is built to punish the turn; the escape is possible toward the knee-up side, but the counters are the back and the armbar.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Technical mount is a high-risk spot where the elbow escape still recovers half guard on the knee-down side, but failed turns feed the back take and the armbar.

guard-back.reason: Turning into the top player and elbow-kneeing to half guard is the right answer but it is a high-risk spot; turning the wrong way gives the back, and an extended arm gives the armbar.

gi-guard-modern.reason: You are already half-turned and the arm is exposed, so the escape is hard and counters split between the back take and the armbar.

unorthodox.reason: You are already on your side with a knee by your head, so re-guarding is harder than the anchor; failing to flatten back gives the back or the near-arm armbar.

gi-to-nogi.reason: You are already on your side, but the leg by your head blocks the frame, and turning further gives up the back or the armbar.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Turning to shrimp in technical mount is exactly what feeds the back take or the armbar, so it is a low-percentage re-guard; no-gi riders punish the turn with the back more.

systems.reason: Peeling the wrist across from the seat belt to trap the arm is a common back attack, slightly under the mount rate; letting go of the seat belt lets some defenders turn in, and no-gi wrists slip out more.

pragmatist.reason: Trapping an arm across from the back is a real choke setup but they are hand-fighting for exactly that arm; below the mount odds, and sleeve grips help in the gi.

leg-skeptic.reason: Trapping the arm across the neck from the seat belt is a niche arm-trap move and well below the mount figure. A wrist slips more easily in no-gi, and when you give up the hand-fight they turn in.

academic.reason: Pulling the far wrist across from the seat belt is a real back-attack trap, but the hands are fighting, so it lands well below the mount version; sleeves make it easier in gi, and loosening the seat belt invites a turn-in escape.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: His hands fighting at the neck are there to be trapped across his body from the seatbelt, and a sleeve grip makes it easier in the gi; reaching for the wrist is where he turns into you in no-gi.

guard-back.reason: The far-wrist trap across the neck from the seatbelt is a standard back-attack chain; the sleeve makes feeding the wrist easier in gi; loosening the belt line to do it is when they turn in.

gi-guard-modern.reason: From the seatbelt you trap the far wrist across and roll them to a mounted gift wrap; wrist and sleeve grips help in gi, and releasing the belt lets some escape into your half guard.

unorthodox.reason: Trapping a hand-fighting arm across the body from the seat belt is a known back attack, harder than from mount since the hands are busy at the neck; the lapel trap makes it easier in gi.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Gift wrap is back control with an arm trapped, so from the seat belt it is a short step; the gi adds lapel arm-traps, while in no-gi a sweaty wrist slips the trap and the turn-in escape comes more often.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Win the wrist off the seat belt and feed it across to the far hand. It is real but harder than from mount, and freeing a hand lets them slide out the back and come up on top.

systems.reason: Chill dog's compact shell sets up the shoulder roll much like turtle; collar grips stop the roll a little more often in gi, and a mistimed roll gives the back.

pragmatist.reason: The chill dog traps your near arm, so the granby is harder than from plain turtle; better without collar grips.

leg-skeptic.reason: Chill dog is a compact turtle, so the Granby works about the same as from turtle; collar grips slow the roll in gi.

academic.reason: The compact shell sets up the shoulder roll about as well as plain turtle; collar and belt grips stall the roll in gi, and Granby rolls are more common in no-gi.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: This is a compact turtle, so the granby runs near canonical; in the gi, collar and belt grips stop the roll a little more often.

guard-back.reason: A compact turtle with the rider beside you rolls much like plain turtle, so odds are about canonical; gi collar/belt grips stop the roll slightly more, and a stalled granby exposes the back.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Compact like a turtle, so the granby recovery works much as it does canonically; gi belt and collar grips let the top player block the roll and take the back.

unorthodox.reason: Chill dog's compact shell is a good launch for a Granby, close to the turtle canonical. Collar grips stop the roll more in the gi, and a slow roll gives up the back.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Chill dog is built to feed the granby; the roll is freer in no-gi, while gi collar and belt grips stop it more often.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Chill dog is a compact turtle, so the granby runs near the turtle baseline; no-gi rolls more freely but lands open guard more often.

systems.reason: Peeling a locked gable grip is the first body-lock defence but much harder than breaking guard grips; the gi lets the attacker reinforce through the belt, and no-gi sweat helps the peel.

pragmatist.reason: Peeling a locked body lock is much harder than stripping guard grips; while you work the hands they mat-return or circle to the back.

leg-skeptic.reason: Peeling a locked body lock two-on-one is far harder than stripping open-guard grips, and while you work the hands they mat-return you.

academic.reason: A two-on-one peel on a locked body lock is harder than an open-guard grip break; while you work the hands, the attacker mat-returns you.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: A locked body lock is far stronger than open-guard grips; in the gi the opponent can also hold the belt or jacket, so stripping it works less often.

guard-back.reason: Peeling locked hands around your waist is far harder than stripping a guard grip; while you work the hands they can lift for the mat return.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Locked hands are harder to peel than open-guard grips; in the gi the attacker can switch to a belt grip, so gi is lower.

unorthodox.reason: A locked body lock is far harder to strip than open-guard grips; a failed peel invites the mat return.

gi-to-nogi.reason: A locked body lock is far harder to strip than an open-guard grip; in the gi they can also anchor on the belt.

fhl-scrambler.reason: A gable or S-grip around the waist is much harder to peel than open-guard grips, and in the gi they can switch to the belt; a failed peel gets you mat-returned.

systems.reason: Fighting the heel grip is essential honey hole survival, but the entanglement stays on, so freedom is rarer than in open guard; the attacker switches to the toe hold or the back.

pragmatist.reason: Hand-fighting the heel grip is the core of honey-hole defense; it works less often in no-gi where the heel hook is live.

leg-skeptic.reason: Hand-fighting the heel is THE leg-lock defence, but a stripped grip only buys time until you clear the knee line or counter-entangle; elite no-gi attackers re-grip fast.

academic.reason: Stripping the heel grip mostly buys safety inside the entanglement, as in the canonical table; elite no-gi leg lockers re-grip and punish more.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Two-on-one stripping the heel grip is the first survival step but the entanglement holds; no-gi heel control is tighter and better drilled.

guard-back.reason: Hand-fighting the heel grip is the core honey-hole defense; it usually only buys time inside the entanglement, and turning to escape gives backside 50-50.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Stripping the heel grip buys safety but rarely frees the leg; gi pants give the attacker a sticky alternate grip, sweat helps in no-gi.

unorthodox.reason: Stripping the heel grip is core leg-lock defence and usually works, but it often just leaves you safer inside the entanglement; turning to free hands gives backside 50-50, more in no-gi.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Stripping the heel grip protects the heel but rarely frees the leg; the defensive turn can feed backside 50-50.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Two-on-one on the heel grip buys time, but clearing the leg against an inside sankaku is hard; turning the wrong way hands them the backside.

systems.reason: Standard half guard passing mechanics do not work with the bottom player under your hips; you must first kill the deep half, so success drops and waiter sweeps rise.

pragmatist.reason: You must dig them out before passing; deep half is a sweeping guard, so the counter rate is high.

leg-skeptic.reason: They are under your hips; you must drag them out to regular half before passing, and the waiter-style sweeps are live the whole time.

academic.reason: Deep half takes away the crossface and underhook battle a standard half-guard pass relies on, and waiter sweeps punish it; slightly worse in no-gi.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Bottom is under the hips with sweeps loaded, so passing is harder than from plain half; gi grips to flatten help a little.

guard-back.reason: Deep half bottom is under your hips with high-percentage sweeps; passing is well below canonical, occasionally the turn-away gives the back.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Bottom is under the hips with sweep leverage, so passing is below canonical; gi collar crossface helps top, belt grip helps the waiter sweep.

unorthodox.reason: With them under your hips the waiter-style sweeps are live, so the pass lands less and the counter rate rises.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Opponent is under the hips and off-balancing constantly; passing first needs a whizzer and backstep, sweeps are common.

fhl-scrambler.reason: You first have to flatten them back out of deep half; waiter sweeps and backdoor back takes punish a premature pass, especially in no-gi.

systems.reason: The figure-four on the trapped leg has to be broken before any pass; gi crossface and belt grips help the top a little more than no-gi.

pragmatist.reason: The lockdown kills the knee-cut and leg-pull until it is broken; most attempts stall there.

leg-skeptic.reason: The lockdown has to break before a half guard pass exists; no-gi lockdown players are better at it, and a gi crossface helps the passer.

academic.reason: The leg must be extracted from the figure-four before any half-guard pass; gi collar crossface helps a little, and old-school sweeps are the counter.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: The figure-four lockdown must be broken before any pass, so it is below canonical; the lockdown is a no-gi weapon and less effective against gi pressure.

guard-back.reason: The figure-four on the leg must be broken first; many attempts only free the leg back to half guard, and the stretch opens the old school sweep or back.

gi-guard-modern.reason: The figure-four must be broken before the pass; gi collar control makes flattening the bottom player slightly easier.

unorthodox.reason: The lockdown stalls the extraction; most misses stay locked or drift to plain or deep half, and the old school/plan B sweeps punish posting.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Leg must be extracted from the figure-four first; gi grips aid the crossface while the lockdown system is sharper in no-gi.

fhl-scrambler.reason: The figure-four has to be unlocked before any half guard pass; a cleared lockdown that stays half guard is the common miss.

systems.reason: Whizzer and crossface give near-canonical passing control, but the old school sweep is exactly what a miss feeds, more so in no-gi.

pragmatist.reason: Whizzer and crossface give the top a fair passing platform, roughly canonical, but the old-school sweep is live.

leg-skeptic.reason: Whizzer and crossface keep this near the half guard baseline, but the deep underhook makes the old school sweep and the back take real counters.

academic.reason: Whizzer plus crossface blunts the old-school sweep, so the pass sits just under the canonical half-guard rate.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Whizzer and crossface are already set, which puts the passer ahead of plain half guard; the old-school sweep remains the main counter.

guard-back.reason: Whizzer and crossface give real control, so slightly below canonical; losing the whizzer while passing feeds the old school sweep or back take.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Whizzer and crossface already established, so close to canonical; the old-school sweep stays the main counter.

unorthodox.reason: Crossface and whizzer are already in, so the pass is near-canonical, but the old school sweep is a high-percentage answer to a posted foot.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Whizzer and crossface already flatten the bottom player, so the pass lands slightly above canonical; old school sweep is the risk.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Whizzer and crossface already flatten them, so the pass is near canonical, but the old-school sweep is the live counter and nastier in no-gi.

systems.reason: The lockdown plus whip-up must be dismantled before the half guard pass can run, so success is well under canonical and sweeps and back takes are live.

pragmatist.reason: Leg locked down with the whip-up threat; passing before killing the lockdown gets swept or back-taken.

leg-skeptic.reason: From under a whip-up you are surviving, not passing; most wins are just killing the lockdown back to plain half.

academic.reason: A lockdown with whip-up is a harder half guard; you usually flatten them back to plain half guard before passing.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Lockdown plus whip-up makes a straight half guard pass low-percentage; the usual gain is only to clear back to plain half.

guard-back.reason: Must flatten and kill the whip-up before a half guard pass is possible; the vaporizer sweep punishes a light base, slightly more in no-gi.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Trapped in lockdown and being whipped up, the pass is well below canonical; partial success only returns to standard half guard.

unorthodox.reason: The whip-up elevates you before you can extract; killing it resets to half guard top, a miss is swept or loses the back.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Lockdown plus whip-up keeps the top player off base; extraction to mount is the cleanest finish, sweeps are frequent in no-gi.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Lockdown with whip-up off-balance means you are passing from a broken base; well below the plain half guard rate.

systems.reason: You already hold the leg, so switching to the inside position is easier than entering from open guard; no-gi leg lockers drill this switch constantly.
