gi-to-nogi.reason: Passing to the side while one arm holds the neck is a real finishing angle, but a one-armed pass is slower; a stalled attempt costs the grip and leaves you in guard, and their head pop can reverse you.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Their hands are busy defending the neck, so walking around to side control is easy; if you let the head go too early they re-guard.

systems.reason: Booting the foot and passing as they fall back is the standard counter to a straight ankle lock; no-gi attackers chain into inside ashi more readily.

pragmatist.reason: Defend the ankle, step over and pass is a staple; in no-gi the attacker more often switches to inside ashi and the heel as you move.

leg-skeptic.reason: Boot the foot, clear the knee and pass on a player who fell back for a footlock: legit and common. No-gi leg lockers punish it by switching to inside ashi far more often.

academic.reason: Stepping over to pass from a straight ankle defense works but the leg is still caught; no-gi bottom players punish the step with an inside-ashi heel-hook switch more often.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Clearing the foot and stepping over to side control works when he falls back for the ankle lock; the no-gi attacker's switch to inside ashi punishes it more often.

guard-back.reason: Booting the foot, stepping over and passing is the standard SAL counter-pass; often you free the leg but only reach open guard, and the step-over feeds inside ashi, more so in no-gi.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Stepping over and passing as they fall back for the ankle lock is a standard defence; pants friction slows the foot slip in gi, and no-gi attackers switch to inside ashi more.

unorthodox.reason: Boot-and-pass out of a straight ankle lock is a known escape but the foot is still trapped; no-gi attackers switch to inside ashi faster.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Boot, sit up and step over to pass is the classic answer to a straight ankle lock, but you start inside the attack. In no-gi the attacker re-wraps to inside ashi for heel hooks far more often.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Boot, clear the foot and step over to pass is the textbook defence; in no-gi, stepping over gets punished by the switch to an inside heel hook.

systems.reason: The stack-and-pass triangle escape is real but riskier than a pass from neutral; the triangle player answers with the armbar switch or rolls you into a mounted triangle.

pragmatist.reason: The stack pass out of a triangle is real but you are fighting with your head trapped; it fails often and the guard player switches to the armbar or sweeps.

leg-skeptic.reason: The stack pass out of a triangle is the textbook escape; pant grips help stack in gi, and the armbar switch is the standard punishment for a lazy stack.

academic.reason: A stack pass out of a triangle relies on pants and belt grips in gi; a pass that goes wrong hands them the armbar switch or the triangle sweep.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Posture, stack and walk to the side is the textbook triangle-escape pass, but it fails often; the punish is the armbar switch or the roll to mounted triangle.

guard-back.reason: Stack pass out of a half-locked triangle works often but they re-close guard, switch to the armbar or lock the triangle on the stack; pant grips help the stack slightly in gi.

gi-guard-modern.reason: The stack pass out of a triangle; collar and sleeve grips hold the triangle and the armbar switch tighter in gi, while legs slip more in no-gi.

unorthodox.reason: The stack pass is the standard triangle escape; pant grips help in gi, slipperier legs help in no-gi, and a bad stack gets armbarred or triangle-swept.

gi-to-nogi.reason: The stack pass to the trapped-arm side is the textbook triangle escape. The gi's friction and collar grip keep the triangle tighter, and a failed stack hands them the armbar switch or a roll into mounted triangle.

fhl-scrambler.reason: The stack pass to side control is the standard triangle escape; a stack that runs too high gets the armbar, and loose posture lets them lock the triangle.

systems.reason: Smashing the butterfly hook flat is the main answer to butterfly half; slightly below canonical because the hook gives elevation, a bit lower in no-gi without crossface/belt grips.

pragmatist.reason: Flatten-and-smash is the staple answer to butterfly half; the hook still elevates, more so without gi grips to pin.

leg-skeptic.reason: Flatten, kill the hook, crossface: a real answer here, but the butterfly lift punishes lazy forward weight, more so without gi friction.

academic.reason: Flattening and killing the butterfly hook is the standard answer; gi crossface grips help, no-gi butterfly-half sweeps punish more.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Flattening the butterfly hook with heavy hips works a bit below canonical; the hook-elevation sweep is the main punishment, stronger in no-gi.

guard-back.reason: Flattening the butterfly hook and crossfacing works near canonical; the live hook makes the elevation sweep a bigger counter, more so in no-gi.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Smashing flat kills the hook but the half-guard trap remains; gi crossface/belt grips help top slightly, no-gi hook elevation punishes more.

unorthodox.reason: Smashing the butterfly hook flat is the right answer here, but the hook elevates you into sweeps more than combat base does, worse in no-gi.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Flattening kills the hook but the trapped leg slows the pass; gi pant and collar grips pin hips better than no-gi.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Flattening to kill the hook is the right answer here, but the butterfly elevation punishes leaning in, more so in no-gi without pant/belt grips.

systems.reason: Active double butterfly hooks punish forward weight with elevation sweeps; flattening often stalls in half guard, so success sits under canonical.

pragmatist.reason: Must flatten active hooks first; pressure often stalls in half guard and leaning in feeds the butterfly sweep.

leg-skeptic.reason: Driving weight into live butterfly hooks is what the guard player wants; hooks must die first, so lower than from combat base.

academic.reason: Double butterfly hooks are built to elevate forward pressure, so the pass rate drops below combat base and sweep risk rises, more so in no-gi.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Driving pressure into active double hooks risks the elevation sweep; gi grips on collar and belt make the flattening slightly more reliable.

guard-back.reason: Both hooks active means you must kill a hook before the pressure lands; misses often stall in half guard, and leaning in feeds the butterfly sweep.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Flattening is the standard answer to hooks, near canonical; a mistimed drive feeds the butterfly elevation, more so in no-gi scrambles.

unorthodox.reason: Two active hooks punish committed weight; a flattened miss ends in half guard, an overcommit gets elevated to mount.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Smashing active hooks works but every lean feeds the elevator; butterfly sweeps bite harder without gi friction.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Two live hooks make forward pressure a sweep invitation; a stalled smash usually ends in top half, an overcommitted one gets elevated.

systems.reason: The leg hook already controls the defending leg, so heavy hip-to-hip pressure finishes the half guard pass more often than from combat base.

pragmatist.reason: Leg already hooked and half-passed, so heavy pressure finishes the pass more often than from combat base.

leg-skeptic.reason: The leg is already hooked and the pass half done, so smashing through beats the combat-base number.

academic.reason: The bottom leg is already hooked and half the pass is done, so pressure finishes above the canonical rate.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: The leg is already hooked and the pass is half done, so finishing with pressure beats the canonical rate; crossface and lapel grips help most in the gi.

guard-back.reason: The hooked leg already pins the bottom leg, so the pressure pass is above canonical and occasionally slides straight to mount.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Leg already hooked and controlled, so pressure finishes the half-guard pass above canonical; gi pants grip keeps the leg pinned a bit better.

unorthodox.reason: The leg is already hooked and half the pass is done, so heavy pressure finishes more often than from combat base.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Leg already hooked and hips half-cleared, so pressure finishes the pass more often than from combat base.

fhl-scrambler.reason: The leg is already hooked and half the pass is done, so pressure finishes above the canonical rate.

systems.reason: With an arm overhooked and posture broken, a direct stack-and-pass rarely clears the guard and driving forward feeds the triangle.

pragmatist.reason: Arm trapped and posture broken; stacking through New York is low-percentage and pushing in feeds the triangle.

leg-skeptic.reason: With posture broken and an arm trapped you stack-smash or you eat a triangle; nobody pressure passes cleanly out of New York.

academic.reason: With an arm trapped and posture broken you must recover posture before pressure works; driving in feeds triangles, more so for no-gi rubber-guard specialists.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: With an arm overhooked and posture broken you must stack before passing; pushing forward with an arm trapped feeds the triangle, which is less sticky in the gi.

guard-back.reason: Trapped arm and broken posture must be fixed first; stacking pressure into the New York often feeds the triangle, worse in no-gi where the rubber guard grips are stickier relative to top's grips.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Posture is broken and an arm is overhooked, so a stack-pressure pass rarely completes; gi belt/pant grips make the stack slightly more viable.

unorthodox.reason: Stack-passing is the real threat to New York, but with an arm trapped and posture broken it rarely gets through, and stacking feeds the triangle.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Posture broken and arm trapped; stacking through rubber guard rarely clears it and feeds the triangle.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Arm trapped and posture broken; stack-smashing can work but driving forward into New York feeds the triangle.

systems.reason: Essentially the canonical situation without a settled combat base; pressure passing from generic open guard top performs near canonical, with half guard as the common stall.

pragmatist.reason: Essentially the canonical situation; slightly harder to pin a slippery no-gi guard player, misses often stall in half.

leg-skeptic.reason: Close to the combat-base case once you close distance; no-gi guards are slipperier and harder to pin.

academic.reason: Close to the combat-base origin; misses mostly leave you in open guard or stuck in half guard, and no-gi open guards are a bit more mobile.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Generic open guard plays like the canonical origin; gi friction and grips favour the pressure passer, while no-gi lets the bottom player slip and re-guard.

guard-back.reason: Generic open guard top is close to combat base, so near canonical; failures stay in open guard or get trapped in half, counters are sweeps.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Essentially the canonical situation; gi sleeve/collar distance grips slow the close slightly, and half-guard recovery is the common miss.

unorthodox.reason: Generic open guard is close to the canonical setting; no-gi legs are harder to pin, and partial passes stall in half guard.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Near the canonical combat-base entry but with more distance to close; no-gi hips slip out from under the pin.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Generic open guard is close to the canonical combat-base setup; stalled pressure passes most often get caught in half.

systems.reason: Stacking is a standard rubber guard defence but posture is broken and the arm isolated, so passing outright is low and forward pressure invites triangles, slightly more so in no-gi.

pragmatist.reason: Posture is compromised under rubber guard; stack-pressure works sometimes but driving in exposes the triangle.

leg-skeptic.reason: Stacking through rubber guard is the textbook answer but feeds triangles; a gi lets top grip and posture a bit better.

academic.reason: Stacking pressure is the textbook rubber-guard answer, but posture is compromised and the triangle threat is constant.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Stacking is the right answer to rubber guard but the posture break comes first, so it is well below canonical; the triangle counter is a bigger threat in no-gi.

guard-back.reason: Posture is broken by the high guard, so pressure must first strip the leg; gi collar/belt grips help top recover posture slightly more than in no-gi.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Must recover posture before any pressure works; rubber guard is weaker in the gi where top can grip pants and stack, stronger in no-gi.

unorthodox.reason: Posture-then-stack beats rubber guard more than anything else does, but from inside the clamp it fails often and walks into triangles; gi collar grips help the posture.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Must recover posture before any pressure; gi belt and collar grips help the stack, sweaty no-gi favours the rubber guard.

fhl-scrambler.reason: You need posture before you can pressure; passing straight from broken posture is low percentage and triangle-prone.

systems.reason: Flattening and crossfacing is the right anti-lockdown idea, but the whip-up and underhook make a full pass hard and expose sweeps and back takes.

pragmatist.reason: Flattening is the right answer to the lockdown whip-up but the leg is still locked; gi grips help the top pin.

leg-skeptic.reason: Old-school flatten-and-crossface beats the lockdown, but once the whip-up is in your base is gone and back exposure is real.

academic.reason: You must kill the whip-up and free the locked leg before pressure can finish; many attempts only flatten them back to half guard.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: With a leg in the lockdown and the whip-up live, pressure usually only flattens to plain half guard; the full pass is rare.

guard-back.reason: Lockdown plus whip-up keeps the base light; flattening often only reaches half guard top, and over-committing feeds the whip-up sweep or back take.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Lockdown plus whip-up means the leg must be freed first; crossface pressure is the right idea but often only gets back to plain half guard.

unorthodox.reason: You cannot pass a locked-down leg; flattening kills the whip-up and leaves half guard, and a heavy miss is swept or gives up the back.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Crossface and whizzer pressure is the right answer but the lockdown pins the leg and the whip-up punishes heavy weight.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Lockdown plus whip-up makes base the first problem; the gi gives a little more crossface and belt control to flatten them.

systems.reason: The trapped arm must be freed before weight can pin the hips; stacking passes sometimes, but a miss often feeds the shoulder-lock or omoplata chain.

pragmatist.reason: Stacking pressure is a real Williams defense but the trapped arm keeps the shoulder-lock and omoplata live.

leg-skeptic.reason: The arm has to come out before any pass, so most attempts only get you back to closed guard top, and driving in feeds the omoplata.

academic.reason: Pressure helps against the shoulder lock, but the arm must come out first; failure usually leaves you in closed guard, and a counter means an omoplata or a sweep.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Stacking pressure is the classic Williams escape, but the trapped arm limits the pass and the shoulder-lock chain punishes a sloppy drive.

guard-back.reason: The trapped arm must come out before any pressure pass; driving forward with it still caught invites the omoplata roll or a sweep.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Trapped arm and shoulder-lock threat must be cleared before pressure passing; driving in early feeds the omoplata.

unorthodox.reason: The trapped arm must come out before weight can pass; stacking from Williams usually recovers closed guard or feeds the triangle.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Trapped arm must come out first; pressuring with it caught walks into the shoulder lock or omoplata.

fhl-scrambler.reason: With an arm trapped under the shoulder-lock threat, pressure only works once the arm comes free; forcing it hands them the omoplata.

systems.reason: Under a double-unders stack the roll over the shoulder to the knees is one of the easier outs, a little better than from flat side control, but turning into it exposes the back.

pragmatist.reason: Turning to the knees against a stack pass is a common bail-out; easier to scramble in no-gi, and a late turn hands over side control or the back.

leg-skeptic.reason: Turning to the knees while being stacked is a real survival reflex. A half-turn gets pinned as the pass finishes, and turning too far gives up the back.

academic.reason: Turning away under a double-under stack is a standard survival exit and a bit easier than from a settled side control; if it's late, they finish the pass or take the back as you turn.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Turning to the knees under a stack is a real escape, but belt and pants grips slow it in the gi, and turning your back to a double-unders passer feeds the back take.

guard-back.reason: Turning to the knees under a stack is a standard double-unders out; a miss often just finishes their pass, and turning too early hands the back. Turning is easier without gi drag.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Rolling over a shoulder to turtle against double unders is a granby-style exit; belt and pant grips let the gi passer hold the stack a little better.

unorthodox.reason: Turning away from a double-under stack is a standard bail-out and slightly easier than from flat side control; a passer at your hips can still finish the pass or take the back.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Under a double-unders stack, turning onto your knees as they drive over is a real escape; belt and pant grips slow the turn a little in the gi, and a late turn completes their pass.

fhl-scrambler.reason: With your hips stacked, turning in and granbying to turtle is a real exit; a double-under passer is already behind your hips and flows to the back.

systems.reason: Turning away from a leg drag is the instinctive escape but it is exactly what the leg-drag passer wants, so back-take counters run high.

pragmatist.reason: Turning away is the instinct against a leg drag, but the leg drag is built to take the back when you turn; the back-take counter is heavy.

leg-skeptic.reason: Turtling is the common answer to a leg drag, but the drag-to-back is the passer's whole plan, so the counter mass sits above the side-control figure.

academic.reason: Turning away is the natural reaction to a leg drag, and the hip is already turned, which helps; but leg-drag passers are waiting for that turn to take the back, more so in no-gi.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Turning away from a leg drag is the instinctive escape, and the leg drag is built to take the back exactly when you do it, so the counter weight stays high.

guard-back.reason: The leg drag already turns your hips away, so turtling is the easiest response, but leg drag to back take is its main follow-up, so the counter mass stays high, more so in no-gi.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Turning away from the leg drag gets to turtle but hands the back to a ready passer; collar and pant grips make that back take likelier in gi.

unorthodox.reason: Turning in to turtle is the usual answer to a leg drag, but the leg drag already exposes the back, so the back-take counter stays heavy.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Turning away from a leg drag is the natural reaction, but the leg drag is built to take the back of a turtling opponent, so the back-take counter is heavier than from side control.

fhl-scrambler.reason: The leg drag turns you anyway, so turtling is the natural escape; leg-drag passers are set up for exactly that back take, so the counter is heavy.

systems.reason: The opponent has already conceded back exposure and an arm is tied up, so the roll lands the back a bit more often than from a raw turtle.

pragmatist.reason: The bottom player has accepted back exposure, so rolling to the back is a real option, but you are still inside a deep-overhook rubber guard; a failed roll gets you reversed. Gi belt grip helps the roll.

leg-skeptic.reason: Rolling for the back while your head is trapped in rubber guard is a lottery ticket; only works when they turn away, and rolling feeds the omoplata.

academic.reason: Bottom's angle concedes some back exposure, but the deep overhook ties up the rolling arm, so this is a niche, low-percentage roll; failures fall back into guard.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: The overhooking guard player only partly exposes the back, so the roll is a lower-percentage gamble than from turtle; misses leave you in their guard, bad rolls end underneath.

guard-back.reason: The back is exposed, but the overhook and the leg over your shoulder make rolling over a scramble; that roll feeds their omoplata chain, which no-gi rubber-guard players hit more.

gi-guard-modern.reason: You are inside a rubber-guard overhook, so a roll works only off their turn-away; the gi belt grip helps a little, and failed rolls let them follow you over.

unorthodox.reason: Rolling while your head is pinned in a rubber guard is niche; the bottom man gives the back on purpose, and in no-gi he usually takes yours as you roll.

gi-to-nogi.reason: The back is exposed, but the deep overhook ties up the rolling arm, so this sits well below the turtle origin. A bad roll walks into the omoplata.

fhl-scrambler.reason: The bottom player's deep overhook makes rolling over the shoulder awkward, so it only works when they over-turn; a bad roll lands you underneath or gives up your own back.

systems.reason: Both hooks are already inside the thighs so the roll mostly just finishes the seat; gi belt grips steady it, no-gi hooks slip out more.

pragmatist.reason: Both hooks are already in from turtle, so rolling through to the back is the intended follow-up and better than from plain turtle; the counter is them rolling you into their half guard.

leg-skeptic.reason: Both hooks already inside the turtle, so the roll is the natural finish and beats the bare-turtle anchor; gi belt grip helps keep them on the roll.

academic.reason: Both hooks are already in, so the roll mostly finishes the back take; it is above the turtle-top rate. No-gi loses the belt grip that steers the roll, matching the canonical gi-over-no-gi gap.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Both hooks are already inside the thighs, so the roll to the back is the natural finish and beats the canonical turtle rate; gi belt and collar grips steer the roll.

guard-back.reason: Both hooks are already inside the thighs, so the roll carries them straight to the back and beats the turtle rate; the gi belt grip helps, and in no-gi they slip out more often.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Both hooks are already inside, so the roll needs little extra; belt and collar grips keep it tight in the gi, and a sloppy roll ends under half guard.

unorthodox.reason: With both hooks already in, the roll just carries them over, so above the anchor; the no-gi back slips more, and a roll-through sometimes leaves you under in half guard.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Both hooks are already in, so the roll mostly just finishes the back take, well above the plain turtle rate. Belt and collar grips steady it in the gi.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Both hooks are already in, so the roll is the natural finish and beats the plain-turtle rate; gi belt and collar grips keep the roll tighter, and in no-gi more opponents follow the roll through and come up on top.

systems.reason: A real follow when the defender turns away to clear the knee line, but releasing the entanglement to roll often just frees the leg.

pragmatist.reason: A real follow when they turn away to clear the knee line, but most people stay on the heel; a bad roll loses the leg and they come on top.

leg-skeptic.reason: Real back take when they turn belly-down to escape the heel exposure, but you give up the leg to chase it; in no-gi most people just finish the heel hook.

academic.reason: The back take off the defender's turn-away from the heel hook is a drilled no-gi leg-lock sequence; the gi population rarely plays it. Misses settle in 50-50 or let the leg free and the passer come on top.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: When the leg-locked opponent turns away, the roll to the back is real but less direct than from turtle; failures keep or loosen the entanglement, and a botched roll lets them come up on top.

guard-back.reason: It is a real follow when they turn away from the heel-hook line, but you give up the entanglement to roll, and a miss lets them come up on top.

gi-guard-modern.reason: You follow their turn-away from the heel exposure to the back; no-gi defenders turn more under heel-hook threat, while the gi belt grip helps the roll itself.

unorthodox.reason: A real, under-rated follow when they turn away from the heel line, sometimes passing through the truck; it only fires when they turn, so slightly under the anchor, and it is a bigger gi option because heel hooks are illegal there.

gi-to-nogi.reason: A berimbolo-style roll to the back works when they turn away from the heel exposure. Pants and belt grips make it cleaner in the gi; in no-gi they spin out more freely.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Saddle to back is a real no-gi chain when the opponent turns away to hide the heel, but only off that reaction; rolling loosens the legs and they can free the leg and come on top.

systems.reason: Following the forward-roll escape onto the back is a standard omoplata branch; belt and lapel grips keep the defender pinned better in gi.

pragmatist.reason: Following their forward roll to the back is a classic omoplata finish branch; in no-gi the arm and hips slip out more, so they posture back to guard more often.

leg-skeptic.reason: Following their forward roll out of the omoplata to the back is a staple follow-up, about the anchor; no-gi arm slips out more.

academic.reason: Following the defender's forward roll to the back is a standard omoplata follow-up; a belt grip helps in gi, and the arm slips out more in no-gi.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Following the omoplata defender's forward roll to the back is a classic gi sequence, near the canonical rate; the belt grip helps in the gi; failed rolls let them come up on top.

guard-back.reason: The omoplata-to-back roll is a staple because they are already bent forward; the gi belt grip makes it a bit better, and their forward roll is the counter.

gi-guard-modern.reason: The omoplata roll-through to the back is a standard chain, and the belt grip on the omoplata anchors it in the gi; a slipped roll lets them come up on top.

unorthodox.reason: Following their forward roll to the back is a standard omoplata branch, close to the anchor; in no-gi the shoulder slips out more and they come up on top.

gi-to-nogi.reason: When they forward-roll out of the omoplata you follow them over onto the back. The gi belt grip that pins the hips is what makes it reliable, so no-gi is lower.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Following the forward roll from the omoplata to the back is a classic chain, and the trapped arm helps; in no-gi the arm slips out more, so they roll free and land in your guard.

systems.reason: With knees at the armpits there is no room to get a knee in; a shrimp mostly just pushes them back to low mount, and turning feeds S-mount; gi collar grips hold high mount better.

pragmatist.reason: Shrimping from high mount mostly fails and opens the arm; you must first get them back to low mount.

leg-skeptic.reason: With knees in your armpits there are no hips to shrimp; turning sideways hands them S-mount, and the best a shrimp usually does is drop them back to low mount.

academic.reason: High knees take away the elbow-knee space, so the shrimp mostly just knocks them back to low mount; turning exposes the arm to S-mount. Gi collar grips punish it more.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: With the knees at your armpits there is no elbow-knee frame and no bridge to load the shrimp; turning on your side feeds the S-mount and armbar.

guard-back.reason: With knees in the armpits there is no knee to shrimp under, so a shrimp at best drops them to low mount; turning to shrimp feeds the S-mount and armbar. Sweat helps a little in no-gi.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Knees at the armpits leave almost no room to hip-escape, and turning to the side feeds S-mount; gi collar grips pin the shoulders even harder.

unorthodox.reason: With the knees at your armpits there is almost no hip space. Turning to shrimp feeds S-mount; at best you knock them back to low mount. Sweat helps a little in no-gi.

gi-to-nogi.reason: Knees at the armpits kill the bridge and the hip; turning to shrimp exposes the arm to an S-mount, and collar grips add to it in gi.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Knees at the armpits leave no elbow-knee space, so shrimping mostly just pushes them back to low mount; they follow the hip into S-mount.

systems.reason: Already on your side, so the hip escape is available, but turning away hands over the back (more in no-gi) or the far arm (more in gi).

pragmatist.reason: Shrimping toward the posted knee works sometimes; turning away hands up the back or the arm.

leg-skeptic.reason: You are already on your side, so there is a gap to hip-escape into, but showing your back or extending the arm is how technical mount ends.

academic.reason: The posted knee leaves some hip space, but technical mount is built to punish the shrimp with a back take or an armbar, so the odds are below canonical.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: Hip-escaping away from the posted knee can win back half guard, but you are already on your side, so a late shrimp gives up the back or the arm.

guard-back.reason: Shrimping toward the down leg to catch half guard is the standard escape, but you are on your side under a back-take/armbar fork, so it lands below canonical with heavy counters.

gi-guard-modern.reason: Shrimping into the gap can recover a guard, but the defender is already on their side, so a mistimed hip escape gives up the back or the arm.

unorthodox.reason: You are already on your side, so a hip escape into half guard is possible, but turning the wrong way gives the back and an extended arm gives the armbar.

gi-to-nogi.reason: The textbook escape: shrimp away from the posted leg to recover guard; turning on your side feeds the back or the armbar.

fhl-scrambler.reason: Hip-escaping toward the posted leg can recover half guard, but turning on your side is exactly what feeds the back take and armbar.

systems.reason: Their hips face your legs, so bridging into them and shrimping a knee back in is the standard escape, near side-control odds; belt grip helps them in gi.

pragmatist.reason: Reverse scarf faces your legs, so hip escape to guard is near canonical; they can step over to mount.

leg-skeptic.reason: Hip escape and knee insertion toward half guard is the standard reverse-scarf escape, about canonical; the top player steps to mount if you over-turn.

academic.reason: In reverse kesa the top player's hips face your legs, so the shrimp to a knee-in half guard is the standard exit at near-canonical odds; a late shrimp lets them step to mount.

gi-fundamentalist.reason: The top player faces your legs, so there is room to shrimp and bring a knee inside, close to the side-control rate; gi belt grips hold you slightly better.

guard-back.reason: Their hips face your legs, so shrimping in to wedge a knee recovers half guard about as often as at side control; they answer by spinning to north-south or stepping to mount.
